title: Inside an SRAM
summary: To understand how a memory fails, you first need to know how it works. This topic opens an SRAM: the 6-transistor cell, how a bit is read and written, and how thousands of cells are organised into an array with decoders, sense amplifiers and column multiplexers.
objectives: Name the six transistors of an SRAM cell and their jobs.
Describe a read and a write step by step, and why a read can disturb a cell.
Explain how an address selects a row and columns in the array.
Compute rows, columns, column-mux ratio and address bits of a word-oriented memory.

blocks.md: One bit of SRAM is stored by **two inverters connected in a loop**: the output of each one drives the input of the other. The loop has two stable states — Q = 0 / QB = 1 or Q = 1 / QB = 0 — and holds it as long as power is on. Two more transistors connect the cell to the outside world.

blocks.hint: Click the parts of the cell.
blocks.caption: Six transistors: two inverters (4) + two access transistors (2)

spots.title: Cross-coupled inverters (M1–M4)
spots.md: Each inverter is one PMOS **pull-up** and one NMOS **pull-down** transistor. Together they form a latch that keeps the bit. This is where the value lives.

spots.title: Storage nodes Q and QB
spots.md: The two internal nodes always hold opposite values. *Reading the cell* means finding out which node is 0.

spots.title: Access transistors (M5, M6)
spots.md: Switches between the storage nodes and the bit lines. They open only when the **word line** is high.

spots.title: Word line (WL)
spots.md: One horizontal wire per **row**. Raising it connects every cell of that row to its bit lines.

spots.title: Bit lines (BL and BLB)
spots.md: Two vertical wires per **column**, carrying the value and its complement. Shared by all cells of the column.

spots.title: Column circuits
spots.md: At the end of each column: **precharge** (pulls both bit lines up before a read), **sense amplifier** (detects a tiny difference), **write driver** (forces a new value).

blocks.md: Follow one cell through a **read** (steps 1–5) and a **write** (steps 6–8). The cell starts holding **0**.

steps.title: 1. The cell holds 0
steps.md: Q = 0, QB = 1. The word line is low: the cell is cut off from the bit lines and just holds its value.

steps.title: 2. Precharge
steps.md: Before a read, both bit lines are charged to **VDD** (logic 1).

steps.title: 3. Word line on
steps.md: The row's word line goes high and M5, M6 open. On the side that stores **0** (Q), the bit line BL starts to discharge through M5 and the pull-down — it drops by only a **small amount ΔV** (around a hundred millivolts) in the short read time.

steps.title: 4. Sense
steps.md: The **sense amplifier** compares BL and BLB. BL is a little lower → the cell holds **0**. The small difference is amplified to a full logic level.

steps.title: 5. Word line off
steps.md: The cell is disconnected again and still holds 0. A read must **never** change the cell — if the access transistor were too strong compared with the pull-down, node Q could rise enough to flip the cell. That failure is a **read disturb** (Topic 6).

steps.title: 6. Write: drive the bit lines
steps.md: To write **1**, the write driver forces BL = 1 and BLB = 0 with strong transistors.

steps.title: 7. Word line on: the cell flips
steps.md: Through M6 the driver pulls QB down. The access transistor must be stronger than the cell's pull-up, so QB falls, the inverters switch and the cell flips: **Q = 1, QB = 0**. If it is too weak, the write fails — a **transition fault** (Topic 4).

steps.title: 8. Word line off
steps.md: The cell now holds 1 on its own.

blocks.title: A delicate balance
blocks.md: Reads need the cell to be **strong** (not to flip); writes need it to be **weak enough** to flip. Defects and process variation can upset this balance — exactly what the fault models of this training describe.

blocks.prompt: Practice: put the steps of a read in order.
items: The bit line on the 0 side drops slightly

subsections.title: The array: decoders and sense amplifiers

blocks.md: Cells are arranged in **rows** (one word line each) and **columns** (one bit-line pair each). Follow an access to a small memory of 32 words × 4 bits:

steps.title: 1. The address arrives
steps.md: 5 address bits for 32 words. The upper bits A[4:2] choose the **row** (8 rows), the lower bits A[1:0] choose a **column group** (4 groups).

steps.title: 2. Row decoder
steps.md: The row decoder turns A[4:2] = 101 into exactly **one** active word line: WL 5. All other word lines stay low.

steps.title: 3. A whole row is opened
steps.md: Every cell of row 5 — all **16** of them — is connected to its bit lines. A row holds **four** words.

steps.title: 4. Column multiplexer
steps.md: The column mux uses A[1:0] = 10 to pick **one column out of every four**: columns 2, 6, 10, 14. These are the 4 bits of the addressed word — they are **interleaved**, not side by side.

steps.title: 5. Read: sense amplifiers
steps.md: Four sense amplifiers amplify the four selected bit-line pairs and drive the data outputs D[3:0].

steps.title: 6. Write: write drivers
steps.md: For a write, the same path works backwards: four write drivers force the selected columns, and only the 4 addressed cells of row 5 are written.

items.title: Why not one column per bit?
items.md: A memory with 1024 words of 4 bits would then be 1024 rows tall and 4 columns wide — a very long, thin block with very long bit lines (slow) and a huge decoder. Folding several words into one row makes the array close to **square**: shorter wires, faster, smaller.

blocks.md:
Real memories are described as **words × bits per word** (e.g. 4096 × 16). The designer chooses the physical shape:

- **cells** = words × bits
- **columns** = cells ÷ rows
- **column-mux ratio** = columns ÷ bits per word
- **address bits** = log₂(rows) for the row + log₂(mux ratio) for the column

blocks.title: Worked example
blocks.md:
A memory of **1024 × 8** bits is built with **128 rows**.

- cells = 1024 × 8 = 8192
- columns = 8192 ÷ 128 = **64**
- column mux = 64 ÷ 8 = **8 : 1**
- address = 10 bits = **7** row bits (128 rows) + **3** column bits (8 groups)

tabs.label: Interleaved bits
tabs.md: With an 8 : 1 mux, the bits of one word sit **8 columns apart**. A particle that hits two neighbouring cells usually damages **two different words**, one bit each — which an error-correcting code (ECC) can fix. Designers interleave on purpose.

tabs.label: Logical vs. physical neighbours
tabs.md: Address 5 and address 6 are neighbours in the **address space**, but in the array they can be far apart (different column groups, or rows that the decoder has scrambled). Many memory faults happen between **physically** neighbouring cells. A good test either knows the real layout (*address scrambling* information) or uses algorithms that do not depend on it — the March tests.

tabs.label: Word-oriented tests
tabs.md: All bits of a word are written at the same time. Faults **between bits of the same word** (intra-word) can only be found if the test writes different values into the bits of one word — using several **data backgrounds** such as 0000, 0101, 0011. You will meet them in the *March tests* training.

questions.text: Which transistors connect the SRAM cell to its bit lines, and what controls them?
options: The two access transistors M5, M6 — controlled by the word line.
The pull-up transistors — controlled by the bit lines.
The pull-down transistors — controlled by the sense amplifier.
All six transistors — controlled by the clock.

questions.text: Put the steps of an SRAM read in order.
items: The bit line on the 0 side drops slightly

questions.text: If the access transistor is too strong compared with the pull-down transistor, a read can flip the cell.
questions.explain: The storage node rises during the read; if it rises too far, the latch switches — a **read disturb**.

questions.text: Why can a write flip the cell although the cell's inverters try to hold the old value?
options: The write driver and access transistor are stronger than the cell's pull-up, so the node is pulled to the new value.
The word line switches off the inverters during a write.
The cell is cleared to 0 before every write.
The sense amplifier stores the new value.

questions.text: A 4096 × 16-bit memory is built with 512 rows. What is the column-mux ratio?
For the same memory (4096 × 16, 512 rows, 8 : 1 mux), how are the 12 address bits split?
questions.explain: 512 rows → 9 bits; 8 column groups → 3 bits; 9 + 3 = 12 (4096 words).

questions.text: What follows from column multiplexing? Select **all** correct answers.
options: The bits of one word are not physically next to each other.
Neighbouring addresses are not always neighbouring cells in the array.
A particle hitting two adjacent cells usually damages two different words.
All bits of a word share one bit line.
